newsitem.title: USA: U.S. raps Arafat, Netanyahu for rhetoric.
newsitem.headline: U.S. raps Arafat, Netanyahu for rhetoric.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday criticised Israeli and Palestinian leaders for attacking each other publicly after she had urged both sides to revive a spirit of partnership on peace.
In a television interview, she repeated her concerns about a "crisis of confidence" in the Middle East and stressed the importance of both sides calming the rhetoric "so there can be a rebuilding."

Albright spoke after Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was quoted in an Israeli newspaper as saying measures imposed by Israel against Palestinians since a suicide bombing last week amounted to a declaration of war, and warned he was preparing accordingly.
"Netanyahu has declared war on us and we have to prepare for what will come. The situation is serious," Arafat was quoted as saying.
Albright, interviewed on the Newshour with Jim Lehrer, said: "Chairman Arafat has commited himself to a peace proces. And that kind of language is not appropriate."
She was also asked about reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the Palestinian Authority of behaving "like a regime facilitating terror, like Iran or Iraq or Libya."
Netanyahu equated economic pressure he exerted on the Palestinians since the bombing with economic sanctions Washington imposed on countries with alleged involvement in terrorism, like Libya.
Albright said this analogy "does not work" and inflames the situation rather than lowering tensions.

"The whole situation is totally different and while we respect the need for a prime minister, Prime Minister Netanyahu, to do what he can to protect the security of the people, using analogies that don't fit don't prove any point," she said.
Asked if the crisis could spin out of control, Albright said, "I think that it's a dangerous situation, but we have seen how the peace process has survived through all kinds of very bad times."
She added that the Israeli and Palestinian leaders faced "hard choices" but their people were committed to peace.
Earlier, State Department spokesman James Rubin also rejected Netanyahu's comparisons, saying "it is hard to fathom how one could compare Chairman Arafat to (Libyan) Colonel (Muammar) Gaddafi."

"Chairman Arafat was on the White House lawn with the president. He signed a peace agreement with the Israelis. We regard him as a partner in our effort to find peace in the Middle East," he said, adding:

Aside from closing the border between Israel and the Palestinian self-rule areas, which stops trade and keeps thousands of Palestinians from jobs in Israel, Israel's treasury has frozen transfer of VAT and customs duties it owes the Palestinians.
Albright has been trying to broker an agreement under which Israel would agree to return the money if Palestinians take specific steps to crack down on terrorism, U.S. officials say.
Albright said the United States would seek to accelerate final status talks on tough issues like Jerusalem and Israeli settlements, while continuing to work on an interim agreement.

But she said repeated U.S. demands for Arafat to arrest suspected extremists, dismantle the infrastructure of the Islamic militant group Hamas, and improve transfer of intelligence information to the Israeli authorities.
